name: The Church household
head: church_thomas

arrival.note: A SOURCE, WHERE THIS PROJECT HAD A GUESS. The block this replaces said so itself — “NOT ATTESTED … 1834 is the earliest year that reading supports and it is a guess”, argued from the date of the store he built rather than from anything about the man. The completed resident-research pass on church_thomas read a published early-Chicago reminiscence as saying that Thomas Church arrived in 1834 and describing his Lake Street building activity. The year does not move; what moves is that it is now a reading with a source, at `inferred` because a reminiscence corroborates an uncommon name, a migration year and a merchant setting without proving the identity. This is the one `arrival` block this pass touches and it qualifies on the stated rule: reconstructed, and citing no source. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source earlier than 1 July 1835 corroborates and dates and never promotes: the person's grade does not move on this.

last_dated_appearance.note: NO SIGHTING, SO THE LEG IS A SOURCE'S SPAN. The card holds no dated reading of this person at or before the scene date; the date here is the far end of what a cited source COVERS, which the role's own note calls the source's bound and not the man's. Read from `roles[] (source_span)` as `1830/1853`, which reaches 1853-12-31 — a window that covers 1835-07-01 itself, so it pins no last sighting before the day and cannot be read as one. THE FIELD IS THE EVIDENCE UNDER THE VERDICT, not a new claim: nothing here moves the presence off `uncertain`, and T-1159 and T-1172 classify this household by this date instead of reading it out of the prose (T-1144 acceptance 9).

married.what_happened: NOT DRAWN FOR THIS HOUSE: MOVED INTO IT. The household model drew this house married and the order book had no woman left in its wife's cell, so no wife was drawn. Honora Fitzgerald headed a house of her own, dealt by T-1174 to fill the women and children the age pyramid lacked; she fits this house by its own rules — her division, a band never above his, no child older than his band allows — and T-2020 folds her house into his: she is his wife here and the 4 of her house come with her. Every name, age band and seed is the one T-1174 drew; the children keep the surname they were dealt with. Both people are the town's invention at the `reconstructed` tier, and the marriage is too: no source says Thomas Church married anybody.

persons.name: Thomas Church

occupation.note: NAMED AS THE BUILDER AND NOT AS THE OCCUPANT, which is all the source says: 'The first store building on Lake Street, a two-story frame structure, was built by Thomas Church.' A man who builds a store is usually a merchant and this record reads it that way one grade down.

persons.note: THE THINNEST DOCUMENTED PERSON IN THE PARCEL AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. The whole of the evidence is one sentence in an uncredited editorial addendum at the foot of a chicagology page, which this project already grades as the weakest text in its own source set. A Thomas Church appears in Andreas's city rosters as an alderman in 1845, ten years past the scene date, which corroborates a man of that name in Chicago and dates nothing here.

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

A TRADE PRINTED IN THE 1839 DIRECTORY, 4 years after the scene, carried here by its crosswalk (T-1254, by tools/derive_resident_roles.py). It is NOT a claim about 1835-07-01 and never becomes one: back-projecting a later volume onto the scene is the defect T-1145 exists to refuse. `place` is the address or place of business the record states in its own column; a firm named only inside the printed line stays in `as_printed` for the business band to rule on. An address NUMBER in the 1839 directory is 1876's and not 1839's, on the compiler's own statement on printed page 3, so `place` carries the street NAME the entry names and the number is dropped — the crosswalk's own `address_rule`, applied here rather than tripped over downstream.

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('church_thomas:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

research_note: A HOUSEHOLD WRITTEN ALMOST ENTIRELY TO KEEP A BUILDING FROM BEING ANONYMOUS, and graded so that a reader can see it. Every field but the name is derived or conjectural. It is kept because an empty building on Lake Street tells a visitor less than a named man with three warnings attached.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. church_thomas, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e0275 (a single entry); church_thomas, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e0611 (a single entry); church_thomas, Norris's Chicago directory of 1844 — n1844_e0340 (a single entry).

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Church, Thomas, grocery and provision store, hi Lake st'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `thomas_church_store`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 4 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1839's evidence and moves nothing.
